# Physical Design with OpenROAD

## Concepts

Physical design optimizes interacting constraints. Higher utilization reduces available whitespace but can increase congestion; long wires can worsen timing; clock distribution adds real insertion delay and skew. A physically reasonable implementation requires more than a logically correct netlist.

A standard-cell library supplies timing and physical views, while the PDK supplies technology rules and models. Analyze results at named operating corners. Power estimates also depend on activity assumptions; area and timing reports alone cannot establish power consumption.

## Implementation

Use the OpenROAD stages invoked by the selected flow to inspect floorplan, placement, clock tree, and routing. Identify large macros, high-fanout controls, long buses, and pin placement constraints.

For the UART case, locate the synchronizer, state machines, counters, and RX-to-TX connection. Relate critical timing paths to these structures. Compare pre-route estimates with post-route results that include interconnect effects.

DRC checks layout against geometric rules. LVS compares extracted connectivity with the expected circuit. Antenna checks and density constraints address additional fabrication concerns. Record these results separately from timing status.

## Hands-on Experiments

Run a baseline and vary one floorplan or utilization choice. Compare cell area, die/core area, congestion, routing completion, and setup/hold results using the same RTL and clock target.

Explain whether a timing change came from logic, cell selection, or routing. Review failures before increasing margins or adding exceptions. Include the selected corner and configuration with every report excerpt.
